# Verified fact bank – WhatsApp status

Rules for using this file:
- **Use only facts from this file.** Every entry here is a well-documented technical/historical fact or a standard
  definition. Do NOT add details, numbers, quotes, names or superlatives that are not written in the entry –
  embellishment is where mistakes creep in.
- Write the Hebrew sentence from the **Say** line. The **Don't say** line lists tempting but wrong/uncertain claims.
- The **Visual** line is the starting idea for the image: the top half must show THIS fact/concept so clearly that someone
  could guess it from the picture alone. You may improve the idea, but it must stay specific to the entry.
  For [cyber-concept] / [code-concept] entries the visual is an **explainer diagram** that shows how it works.
- Any code, command, hash or payload shown in an image must be real and correct (run it / compute it if needed).
- Categories (tags) – the statuses rotate through them in this order (see SKILL.md):
  `attack` → `cyber-concept` → `code-build` → `cyber-tool` → `code-concept` → `cyber-tip` → `history`
- When every id has been used (see history.md), start again from the id used longest ago, with a NEW design.
- The **Archive** section at the end is NOT used for new statuses (off-topic for Tamir's audience).

- **Levels** – each entry has a difficulty level, so the audience is introduced gradually (see SKILL.md "Level progression"):
  `(L1)` basic – anyone gets it, everyday life (passwords, scams, what code can do); `(L2)` intermediate – one new term,
  explained simply; `(L3)` advanced – full technical terms (CVE, XSS, SQL Injection, reverse engineering).

Format: `id` [tag] (L1|L2|L3) — Say: … | Don't say: … | Visual: …
Entries added later also end with `| Source: <url> ; <url>` (see SKILL.md step 1b – two sources required).

## Cyber concepts explained [cyber-concept]

- `ransomware` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: Ransomware is malware that encrypts your files and demands payment for the key. The best protection: regular backups kept offline, and keeping systems updated. | Don't say: that paying always returns the files. | Visual: explainer – files → lock icons → ransom note with a countdown; a backup drive shield on the side.
- `ddos` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: A DDoS attack (Distributed Denial of Service) floods a website with traffic from many devices at once, so real users can't get in. | Don't say: record sizes. | Visual: explainer – dozens of devices sending arrows into one server, server shows "503 Service Unavailable", a lonely real user waiting.
- `mitm` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: In a "Man-in-the-Middle" attack, the attacker secretly sits between you and the website and can read or change what you send. HTTPS encryption is what protects you from this. | Don't say: that HTTPS makes a site trustworthy. | Visual: explainer – phone ↔ hooded figure ↔ server, readable message turning into scrambled text when a padlock (HTTPS) is added.
- `sql-injection` [cyber-concept] (L3) — Say: SQL Injection: when a website puts what you type straight into a database query, input like `' OR '1'='1` can change the query's meaning and bypass a login. The fix: parameterized queries. | Don't say: that it works on most sites today. | Visual: login form with `' OR '1'='1` in the password field and the resulting SQL query below with the injected part highlighted.
- `xss` [cyber-concept] (L3) — Say: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): an attacker hides JavaScript – like `<script>…</script>` – inside content that other users see, such as a comment, and it runs in their browsers. Sites prevent it by escaping user input. | Don't say: specific victims. | Visual: comment box containing `<script>alert(1)</script>`, a popup appearing in another user's browser.
- `zero-day` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: A "zero-day" is a vulnerability the software maker doesn't know about yet – they've had zero days to fix it, so attackers can use it before there is any patch. | Don't say: prices of zero-days. | Visual: calendar page "DAY 0" with a crack in a shield, a patch still "coming soon".
- `hashing` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: Good websites don't store your password – they store a hash of it: a one-way "fingerprint". The same password always gives the same hash, but you can't turn the hash back into the password. | Don't say: that every site does this; a made-up hash (compute the real SHA-256 if you show one). | Visual: explainer – `123456` → machine "SHA-256" → the real hash `8d969eef6ecad3c29a3a629280e686cf0c3f5d5a86aff3ca12020c923adc6c92`, arrow back crossed out.
- `public-key` [cyber-concept] (L3) — Say: Public-key encryption: you give everyone an open padlock (the public key) – anyone can lock a message with it, but only your private key can open it. This idea protects HTTPS and secure messaging. | Don't say: math details. | Visual: explainer – many open padlocks handed out, one golden private key kept close, a locked box travelling between them.
- `brute-force` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: A brute-force attack tries password after password, automatically, until one works. That's why long passwords, limits on login attempts and two-factor authentication matter. | Don't say: crack times. | Visual: login box with a counter flashing through `aaaa, aaab, aaac…`, attempts counter, a "locked after 5 tries" shield.
- `botnet` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: A botnet is a network of infected computers and devices controlled remotely by an attacker – the owners usually have no idea their device is part of it. | Don't say: sizes. | Visual: one command server with puppet strings to laptops, cameras, routers, each with a tiny red eye.
- `keylogger` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: A keylogger is malware that records every key you press – including passwords and messages – and sends them to the attacker. | Don't say: statistics. | Visual: keyboard with each pressed key flying as a glowing letter into a hidden file `log.txt`.
- `trojan-horse` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: A "Trojan" is malware disguised as a legitimate program – named after the wooden horse in the Greek story of Troy. | Don't say: invented history of the term. | Visual: wooden horse made of an "installer.exe" window, code bugs peeking out of a hatch.
- `firewall` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: A firewall checks network traffic against rules and decides what may pass and what is blocked – like a guard at the gate of the network. | Don't say: that it stops every attack. | Visual: wall of glowing bricks with a gate; green packets pass, red packets bounce, rule list `ALLOW 443 / DENY 23`.
- `vpn` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: A VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and the VPN server, so people on the same network (for example public Wi-Fi) can't see your traffic. It does NOT make you fully anonymous or protect you from malware. | Don't say: that it makes you invisible. | Visual: glowing tunnel from a phone through a café Wi-Fi cloud to a server, an eye outside the tunnel seeing only scrambled data.
- `pentest` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: In a penetration test, companies hire ethical hackers to attack their own systems – with written permission – to find the holes before real criminals do. | Don't say: salaries. | Visual: a signed "Authorization" document + hacker silhouette in a white hat testing doors of a building-shaped server.
- `two-factor` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: Two-factor authentication combines two different kinds of proof: something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or key) or something you are (a fingerprint). A stolen password alone is not enough. | Don't say: statistics. | Visual: three icons – brain/password, phone with code, fingerprint – two of them lighting up to open a lock.
- `cve-ids` [cyber-concept] (L3) — Say: Every publicly known vulnerability gets an ID called a CVE, like CVE-2021-44228 – that's the famous Log4Shell. - `phishing-ph` [cyber-concept] (L2) — Say: "Phishing" is spelled with "ph" as a nod to "phreaking" – the hacking of telephone networks by early hackers. | Don't say: a specific year of the first phishing attack. | Visual: phone handset turning into a fishing hook catching an email.
- `social-engineering` [cyber-concept] (L1) — Say: "Social engineering" means hacking people instead of computers – getting someone to reveal a password or click a link through trust, urgency or fear. | Don't say: names of real hackers. | Visual: puppet strings attached to a phone/email icon, chat bubble "דחוף!".

## Cyber tools [cyber-tool]

- `wireshark` [cyber-tool] (L2) — Say: Wireshark is a free, open-source tool that captures network traffic and shows it packet by packet – used by network engineers and cyber analysts to see what is really happening on the network. It was originally called Ethereal. | Don't say: release year. | Visual: packet list with coloured rows, a shark fin cutting through a stream of packets.
- `nmap` [cyber-tool] (L2) — Say: Nmap is a free network-scanning tool from 1997 that discovers devices and open ports. It even appears in the movie "The Matrix Reloaded", where Trinity uses it. | Don't say: other movie claims. | Visual: radar sweep over a network map, terminal `nmap -sV 10.0.0.1` with `22/tcp open ssh`.
- `kali-linux` [cyber-tool] (L2) — Say: Kali Linux is a free Linux distribution that comes with hundreds of security tools pre-installed – made for penetration testers and security researchers. | Don't say: exact tool count. | Visual: dragon-silhouette terminal with tool icons (nmap, wireshark, burp) orbiting.
- `metasploit` [cyber-tool] (L3) — Say: Metasploit (created in 2003) is a framework with ready-made modules for testing known vulnerabilities – a standard tool for ethical hackers, used only with permission. | Don't say: attack instructions. | Visual: console `msf6 >` with a module tree, shield "authorized testing only".
- `burp-suite` [cyber-tool] (L3) — Say: Burp Suite sits between your browser and a website and lets security testers see and modify every request – a standard tool for testing web applications. | Don't say: prices. | Visual: browser → Burp proxy window intercepting an HTTP request `POST /login` → server.
- `hashcat` [cyber-tool] (L3) — Say: Hashcat is a password-recovery tool that uses the graphics card (GPU) to test huge numbers of guesses against password hashes – security teams use it to check how weak passwords really are. | Don't say: guesses-per-second numbers. | Visual: GPU card glowing with hashes streaming in and one password popping out `found: 123456`.
- `virustotal` [cyber-tool] (L1) — Say: VirusTotal is a free website where you can upload a suspicious file or link and have it checked by dozens of antivirus engines at once. | Don't say: exact engine count; that a clean result means 100% safe. | Visual: file icon in the centre of a ring of scanner shields, results `0/70` style ticks (no exact number).
- `haveibeenpwned` [cyber-tool] (L1) — Say: Have I Been Pwned is a free site (created by Troy Hunt in 2013) where you can check whether your email address appeared in known data leaks. | Don't say: database size. | Visual: search box with an email, results showing leak badges, "Oh no – pwned!" in red.
- `shodan` [cyber-tool] (L2) — Say: Shodan is a search engine for internet-connected devices – instead of websites it finds servers, cameras and routers exposed online. | Don't say: device counts. | Visual: world map with glowing pins of cameras/routers, search bar `port:23`.

## Code concepts [code-concept]

- `variable` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: A variable is a labelled box that stores a value: in Python `age = 15` puts 15 into a box called age – and you can change it later. | Don't say: memory details. | Visual: glowing box labelled `age` with 15 dropping into it, code line above.
- `loop` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: A loop repeats code for you: `for i in range(1000): print("שלום")` prints 1,000 lines in a fraction of a second. | Don't say: exact timings. | Visual: circular arrow conveyor printing many lines, counter 1→1000.
- `function` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: A function is a reusable recipe: you write the steps once, give them a name, and run them whenever you need with one line. | Don't say: language-specific claims. | Visual: recipe card `def make_pizza():` with inputs going in and pizzas coming out.
- `if-else` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: `if / else` lets a program make decisions: if the password is correct – log in, else – show an error. That's how every app "decides". | Don't say: n/a. | Visual: flowchart diamond "password correct?" splitting into green "Welcome" and red "Access denied".
- `recursion` [code-concept] (L2) — Say: Recursion is a function that calls itself – each time on a smaller problem – until it reaches a simple case. Programmers' joke: "To understand recursion, you must first understand recursion." | Don't say: who coined the joke. | Visual: nested mirror frames / Russian dolls each containing `factorial(n-1)`.
- `api` [code-concept] (L2) — Say: An API is the way programs talk to each other: a weather app doesn't measure the weather – it sends a request to a weather service's API and gets the data back. | Don't say: specific service names. | Visual: phone app ↔ request/response arrows ↔ cloud server, JSON `{"temp": 24}` coming back.
- `binary-search` [code-concept] (L2) — Say: An algorithm is a precise step-by-step recipe. Binary search, for example, finds an item in a sorted list of 1,000,000 items in at most 20 steps – by halving the list each time. | Don't say: other numbers. | Visual: long sorted bar being cut in half again and again, step counter "1… 20".
- `zero-index` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: In Python and most programming languages, the first item in a list is at position 0, not 1 – so `fruits[0]` is the first fruit. | Don't say: the reason/history. | Visual: row of boxes labelled 0,1,2,3 with fruit icons, `fruits[0]` pointing at the first.
- `open-source` [code-concept] (L2) — Say: Open source means the code is public – anyone can read it, use it and improve it. Linux and Python itself are open source. | Don't say: market-share numbers. | Visual: open glass box of code with many hands adding pieces, Linux penguin + Python snake silhouettes.
- `python-indentation` [code-concept] (L2) — Say: In Python, indentation (spaces at the start of a line) is part of the language itself – it decides which code belongs to which block. | Don't say: "spaces vs tabs" statistics. | Visual: code editor with visible indentation guides highlighted in glow, arrows showing the blocks.
- `byte-8-bits` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: Every letter you type is stored as bits – zeros and ones – and 8 bits make one byte. | Don't say: that every letter is always exactly one byte (Hebrew takes more). | Visual: the letter "A" next to `01000001`, 8 glowing light bulbs on/off.
- `python-zen` [code-concept] (L3) — Say: Typing `import this` in Python prints "The Zen of Python" – 19 short rules for writing good code, like "Simple is better than complex". | Don't say: other rules than real ones (safe: "Beautiful is better than ugly", "Simple is better than complex", "Readability counts"). | Visual: terminal with `>>> import this` and the first lines of the Zen.
- `python-antigravity` [code-concept] (L2) — Say: Typing `import antigravity` in Python opens a famous xkcd comic about Python in the browser. | Don't say: describe the comic in detail. | Visual: terminal `>>> import antigravity` and a stick figure flying above the code.
- `rubber-duck` [code-concept] (L1) — Say: "Rubber duck debugging": explaining your code line by line to a rubber duck often makes you find the bug yourself. | Don't say: statistics. | Visual: yellow duck next to a code editor with a speech bubble.
- `git-linus` [code-concept] (L3) — Say: Linus Torvalds created Git in 2005 – in a few weeks – to manage the Linux source code. | Don't say: exact number of days. | Visual: branching git graph (commits as dots, branches merging) with "2005".

## Cyber tips [cyber-tip]

- `password-123456` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: "123456" keeps appearing at the top of lists of the most common leaked passwords. | Don't say: "the most common password in the world" as a single-source fact. | Visual: open padlock + password field `123456`.
- `password-length` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: Every extra character in a password multiplies the number of possible combinations – so length beats "complicated". | Don't say: specific crack times. | Visual: password bars growing exponentially with each added character.
- `passphrase` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: A passphrase of several random words is easier to remember and much harder to guess than a short "complex" password. | Don't say: crack-time numbers. | Visual: four random word tiles (e.g. "סוס" "שמש" "מטרייה" "גיטרה") forming a lock.
- `2fa-google` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: In a Google study (2019), adding a recovery phone number for a code blocked 100% of automated bot attacks on accounts. | Don't say: "100% of all attacks". | Visual: phone showing a 6-digit code, a robot bouncing off a shield.
- `https-lock` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: The padlock in the address bar means the connection is encrypted – not that the website is honest. Phishing sites can have a padlock too. | Don't say: statistics. | Visual: browser bar with a padlock and a suspicious lookalike address `paypa1.com`.
- `backup-321` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: The 3-2-1 backup rule: keep 3 copies of important files, on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy somewhere else (offline or in the cloud). That's the best answer to ransomware. | Don't say: statistics. | Visual: three file copies – laptop, external drive, cloud – connected by glowing lines, "3-2-1".
- `deepfake-voice` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: Scammers can use AI to clone a person's voice. - `human-factor` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: Most data breaches involve a human element – a click, a weak password or a mistake – not a genius hacker. | Don't say: a specific percentage. | Visual: cursor hovering over a "click here" button with a hook behind it.
- `updates-close-holes` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: Most software updates aren't just new features – they often close security holes that attackers already know about. | Don't say: percentages. | Visual: wall with a hole being patched by an "Update" brick.
- `public-wifi-tip` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: On public Wi-Fi, prefer sites with HTTPS and avoid logging in to sensitive accounts – you don't know who else is on the network. | Don't say: that public Wi-Fi is always hacked. | Visual: café Wi-Fi symbol with an eye hiding in the signal waves.
- `qr-phishing` [cyber-tip] (L1) — Say: Scammers sometimes stick fake QR codes on parking meters and posters – before scanning, check where the link really goes. | Don't say: numbers/locations of specific incidents. | Visual: QR sticker peeling off revealing another QR underneath, warning triangle.

## Cyber & code history [history]

- `first-bug-moth` [history] (L1) — Say: In 1947 operators of the Harvard Mark II found a real moth stuck in a relay and taped it into the logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found". | Don't say: that this invented the word "bug" – say the story made it famous. | Visual: vintage logbook page with a taped moth, relay panel lines.
- `creeper-virus` [history] (L1) — Say: Creeper (1971), considered the first computer worm/virus, did no damage – it only displayed "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can!". | Don't say: that it spread worldwide. | Visual: retro CRT with the message.
- `reaper` [history] (L2) — Say: Soon after Creeper, a program called Reaper was written to chase it and delete it – often called the first antivirus. | Don't say: exact date. | Visual: two pixel creatures – one fleeing, one chasing – across a network map.
- `elk-cloner` [history] (L2) — Say: Elk Cloner (1982), one of the first viruses to spread "in the wild", was written by a 15-year-old as a prank on the Apple II – it showed a short poem. | Don't say: invented lines of the poem (safe to quote only: "Elk Cloner: The program with a personality"). | Visual: floppy disk + Apple II-style screen.
- `brain-virus` [history] (L2) — Say: Brain (1986), considered the first PC virus, was written by two brothers in Pakistan – who put their real names, address and phone number inside it. | Don't say: that they were arrested. | Visual: floppy disk + hex dump with a phone icon.
- `aids-trojan-ransomware` [history] (L2) — Say: The first known ransomware, the "AIDS Trojan" (1989), was mailed to victims on floppy disks and demanded payment sent by post. | Don't say: exact ransom amount. | Visual: envelope with a floppy disk and a padlock on files, "1989".
- `enigma-turing` [history] (L1) — Say: During WWII, Alan Turing and the team at Bletchley Park helped break the German Enigma cipher. | Don't say: exact number of lives saved or "ended the war". | Visual: Enigma rotors and keyboard lamps.
- `hacker-mit` [history] (L1) — Say: The word "hacker" originally meant a clever tinkerer – it was used at MIT (Tech Model Railroad Club) for creative technical solutions, not crime. | Don't say: exact year of first use. | Visual: model railroad tracks turning into circuit traces, "MIT".
- `first-bug-bounty` [history] (L2) — Say: Netscape launched one of the first bug bounty programs in 1995 – paying people who found and reported bugs in its browser. Today companies like Google and Microsoft run such programs too. | Don't say: payout amounts. | Visual: bug icon on a reward badge/coin, browser window "1995".
- `spam-monty-python` [history] (L1) — Say: Junk mail is called "spam" after a Monty Python sketch in which the word "spam" is repeated again and again. | Don't say: that the canned meat company named it. | Visual: inbox flooded with identical "SPAM" lines.
- `python-monty-python` [history] (L1) — Say: Python is named after the British comedy group Monty Python, not the snake. | Don't say: invented quotes from Guido. | Visual: code editor `language = "Python"`, theatre masks.
- `python-christmas` [history] (L1) — Say: Guido van Rossum started Python as a hobby project over the Christmas holidays of December 1989. | Don't say: release dates other than "first released in 1991". | Visual: holiday code editor, snowflakes, "1989".
- `javascript-10-days` [history] (L2) — Say: Brendan Eich wrote the first version of JavaScript in about 10 days in 1995. | Don't say: that the whole modern language was made in 10 days. | Visual: calendar with 10 days crossed out and a yellow square with `{ }`.
- `java-oak` [history] (L2) — Say: Java's original name was "Oak", after a tree outside its creator James Gosling's office. | Don't say: other naming legends. | Visual: oak tree whose branches are code brackets, a coffee cup at its roots.
- `linux-hobby` [history] (L2) — Say: In 1991 student Linus Torvalds announced Linux as "just a hobby, won't be big and professional". | Don't say: anything beyond that quote. | Visual: old Usenet message window with the quote, penguin silhouette.
- `hello-world` [history] (L2) — Say: The "Hello, World!" tradition was popularised by Brian Kernighan's C programming book (1978, with Dennis Ritchie). | Don't say: "invented in 1978" – say "popularised". | Visual: terminal printing `hello, world`, C code `printf("hello, world\n");`.
- `ada-lovelace` [history] (L1) — Say: Ada Lovelace published an algorithm for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine in 1843 – a machine that was never fully built – and is often called the first programmer. | Don't say: that she "built a computer". | Visual: brass gears, punched cards, "1843".
- `hopper-compiler` [history] (L2) — Say: Grace Hopper created one of the first compilers (A-0, 1952) – the idea that a computer can translate human-friendly code into machine code. | Don't say: "she invented programming". | Visual: English-like code → arrow → binary, "1952".
- `eniac-six-women` [history] (L1) — Say: The first programmers of ENIAC (1945–46), one of the first general-purpose electronic computers, were six women. | Don't say: weight/size numbers, "the first computer". | Visual: wall of cables and plugboards with six glowing patch cords, "ENIAC 1946".
- `fortran` [history] (L3) — Say: FORTRAN, released by IBM in 1957, was one of the first widely used high-level programming languages – and it is still used in science today. | Don't say: "the first programming language". | Visual: IBM punched card with FORTRAN code, year 1957.
- `cobol-banks` [history] (L3) — Say: COBOL, a language from 1959, still runs many systems in banks and governments today. | Don't say: specific percentages or dollar amounts. | Visual: green-screen terminal next to a modern bank card, "1959 → today".
- `apollo-hamilton` [history] (L2) — Say: Margaret Hamilton led the team that wrote the onboard flight software for the Apollo missions that landed on the moon. | Don't say: "she alone wrote it". | Visual: lunar module outline + moon, "1969".
- `first-website` [history] (L1) — Say: The first website, created by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN, went online in 1991 – at the address info.cern.ch. | Don't say: that it is the same server today. | Visual: retro browser window with URL bar `info.cern.ch`.
- `y2k` [history] (L1) — Say: The Y2K bug: many old programs stored years with two digits, so the year 2000 could be read as 1900. | Don't say: that disasters happened or that it was "fake". | Visual: digital display flipping `99` → `00`, "1900?" ghosted beside "2000".
- `year-2038` [history] (L3) — Say: The "Year 2038 problem": systems that store time as a 32-bit number will overflow on 19 January 2038. | Don't say: that phones/most systems will crash. | Visual: 32 binary digits filling up, countdown "19.01.2038".
- `unix-epoch` [history] (L2) — Say: Most computers count time as seconds since 1 January 1970 – "the Unix epoch". | Don't say: that all computers do. | Visual: counter `0` at 1970-01-01 → huge running number today.
